newsitem.title: UK: World cotton market to reduce oversupply in 1996/9.
newsitem.headline: World cotton market to reduce oversupply in 1996/9.

text.p: The gap between world cotton production and consumption is set to be slashed to 400,000 long tons in 1996-7 from 1.7 million in 1995-6, the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) said in a report.
Production is expected to fall by five percent to 18.9 million tons while demand recovers ground lost the previous year when it fell 1.5 percent to 18.2 million tons.

But the EIU reduced its consumption forecast for the current year by 300,000 tons to 18.5 million tons after lower Chinese exports built up local cotton stocks and on signs of weakening Russian demand.
European Union anti-dumping duties on imports of cotton grey fabrics imposed in November 1996 are likely to cap raw cotton consumption in Asia, the report said.
Demand from Japan, Taiwan amd South Korea is expected to fall sharply while Indonesia and the Philippines could see a small increase in imports.
The EIU said China had reduced the area sown to cotton and current crops had been damaged by natural pests which should slice output by around twenty percent to 3.8 million tons in 1996-7.
Lower yields in Pakistan, stagant output in India and a predicted fifteen percent drop in the Uzbekistan crop would account for much of the global crop contraction, the report said.

According to EIU calculations, a 4.4 percent expansion in U.S. production, strong growth in Egypt, the Sudan and Mexico and a 33 percent increase in the Australian crop to 570,000 tons will help to offset the declines elsewhere.
The EIU predicted that consumption would post a further increase of 2.7 percent, hitting 19 million tons in 1997-8 as China seeks to increase clothing production and relaxes export restrictions.
But output would rebound to reach 19.5 million tons, increasing the gap between production and consumption by a further 100,000 tons in the year, the report said.
